🚀 Build with AI · Step 1 of 7 · 8 min

Tokens and the context window

Count tokens, plan the window as a budget and work out what a request costs.

🔤 A model reads tokens, not words

Before a language model sees your text, a program called a tokeniser cuts it into tokens: words and pieces of words. Every token comes from a fixed list, the model's vocabulary, and has its own number there. The model works only with these numbers.

A common word is usually one token. A rare word is cut into several pieces: “unbelievably” might become un + believ + ably. Punctuation marks are tokens too.

A model's limits and prices are counted in tokens, not in words, so it helps to estimate how many tokens a text has. A rough rule for English text: 100 tokens are about 75 words.

The rule works for ordinary English text. Other languages and program code usually need more tokens for the same amount of text. Models also differ in their tokenisers, so only your model's own tokeniser gives the exact count.

Task. A rough rule for English text: 100 tokens are about 75 words. About how many tokens is an English article of 1500 words?

Show the solution

1500 / 75 = 20, so the article is about 20 · 100 = 2000 tokens. There are more tokens than words, because some words take several tokens and punctuation marks are tokens too. This is only an estimate: the exact number depends on the text and on the model's tokeniser.

🧩 Where the vocabulary comes from: byte-pair encoding

Nobody writes the vocabulary by hand. A widely used method, byte-pair encoding (BPE), builds it from a large collection of texts.

At the start every single character is a token. Count how often each pair of neighbouring tokens appears, and merge the most frequent pair into one new token, everywhere in the text. Then count again and repeat, tens of thousands of times: every merge adds one token to the vocabulary.

Here is the first count for a tiny text. Pairs overlap: in aaa the pair aa is counted twice.

text: aaabdaaabac
pairs: aa aa ab bd da aa aa ab ba ac
counts: aa 4, ab 2, bd 1, da 1, ba 1, ac 1

The name comes from data compression: the method was invented there to replace frequent pairs of bytes. Many real tokenisers also start from bytes, not characters. The merges are learned once, before the model itself is trained, and after that they never change.

Task. In the text aaabdaaabac, which pair of neighbouring characters does byte-pair encoding merge first?

Show the answer

Right answer: aa

aa appears 4 times, more often than any other pair: ab appears 2 times and the rest once each. Byte-pair encoding always merges the most frequent pair, whatever its letters and wherever it stands in the text.

Task. Merge every aa in aaabdaaabac into one new token Z, going from left to right. How many tokens does the text have now?

Show the solution

Each aaa becomes Z a, so the text is Z a b d Z a b a c: 9 tokens instead of 11. The pair was counted 4 times, but it can be replaced only 2 times, because the pairs in aaa overlap. Now the count starts again on the new text, and two merges later the whole piece aaab is a single token.

📚 What the merges give us

After tens of thousands of merges, frequent words have become single tokens. A rare word never gets a token of its own, so it is written with a few smaller pieces: subword tokens.

This is a compromise. A vocabulary of whole words would need millions of entries and would still miss every new word. Single characters can spell anything, but they make a text several times longer.

Pieces of words give both: texts stay short, and no word is left out. The vocabulary has a fixed size: tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand tokens, depending on the model. And the single characters stay in it, so any text can be spelled: a typo, a new name, a word the model has never seen.

“Frequent” means frequent in the texts the vocabulary was built from, and these usually contain more English than any other language. This is one reason why other languages usually need more tokens.

Task. Why do language models split text into pieces of words (subword tokens) and not into whole words?

Show the answer

Right answer: A fixed vocabulary of pieces can spell any word, even a new or misspelled one

A vocabulary of whole words would need millions of entries and would still miss new words, names and typos. Pieces cover everything with a fixed list: a frequent word is one token, a rare one is spelled with several. The price: a text has more tokens than words.

📦 The context window is a budget

A model can work with a limited number of tokens at once: its context window. Everything in one request has to fit into it: your instructions to the model (the system prompt), the conversation so far, the documents you add, the question, and also the answer the model writes.

So the window is a budget: tokens spent on one part are gone for the others, and what does not fit, the model does not see.

Here is a plan for a small window of 8000 tokens (real windows range from a few thousand tokens to a million or more). One line is still empty: you will fill it in on the next screen.

window: 8000 tokens
instructions: 500
question: 300
kept for the answer: 1000
left for documents: ?

Why does the conversation so far count? The model keeps nothing between requests, so a chat application sends the whole conversation again with every new message.

Task. A model has a context window of 8000 tokens. You send instructions of 500 tokens and a question of 300 tokens, and the answer may be up to 1000 tokens long. At most, how many tokens can the documents take?

Show the solution

8000 − 500 − 300 − 1000 = 6200. The room for the answer comes out of the same window as the input, so it is subtracted too. A longer document has to be shortened, or only its most useful parts are sent.

Task. A long chat no longer fits into the context window. What do chat applications usually do so that it can go on?

Show the answer

Right answer: They drop or summarise the oldest messages, so the model no longer sees them in full

The window has a fixed size, and the weights, set in training, do not change during a chat. The model sees only what the application puts into the window again, so the application leaves the oldest messages out or replaces them with a short summary. This is why a chatbot can lose details from the start of a long chat.

🏷️ Tokens are also the price and the waiting time

Model providers usually charge per token, and they count two kinds. Input tokens are everything you send, each time you send it: instructions, conversation, documents, question. Output tokens are everything the model writes in reply, and each usually costs several times more than an input token.

The model writes its answer one token after another, so a long answer also means a long wait.

Prices are usually given per million tokens. Suppose a model costs 2 units (of any currency) per million input tokens and 10 units per million output tokens. A request with 4000 input tokens and 500 output tokens then costs:

input: 4000 · 2 / 1,000,000 = 0.008
output: 500 · 10 / 1,000,000 = 0.005
total: 0.008 + 0.005 = 0.013 units

A model's API (the interface that programs use to call it) usually reports how many input and output tokens each request used, so you can measure them and do not have to guess. Real prices differ from model to model and change often.

Task. A model costs 2 units per million input tokens and 10 units per million output tokens. One request uses 4000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. How many units do 1000 such requests cost?

Show the solution

One request: 4000 · 2 / 1,000,000 = 0.008 units for the input and 500 · 10 / 1,000,000 = 0.005 for the output, 0.013 together. So 1000 requests cost 1000 · 0.013 = 13 units. The same in millions of tokens: 4 · 2 + 0.5 · 10 = 13.

Task. A request has 4000 input tokens at 2 units per million and 500 output tokens at 10 units per million. Which change saves the most money?

Show the answer

Right answer: Sending half as many input tokens

Half the input saves 2000 · 2 / 1,000,000 = 0.004 units per request. Half the output saves 250 · 10 / 1,000,000 = 0.0025. The 250 tokens of instructions save 0.0005 and the greeting 0.0002. An output token costs 5 times more, but this request has 8 times more input tokens: count before you optimise.

Remember

  • A model reads tokens, not words. For English text, 100 tokens are about 75 words; other languages and code usually need more.
  • Byte-pair encoding builds the vocabulary by merging the most frequent pair of neighbouring tokens, again and again. Its pieces of words can spell any text.
  • The context window is one budget for the instructions, the conversation, the documents, the question and the answer. What does not fit, the model does not see.
  • Price and waiting time both grow with the number of tokens, and an output token usually costs more than an input token. Measure where your tokens go before you optimise.
